en: This suffices to dispel the naive image of the contract as a neutral meeting of equivalent wills and to place the problem back where it truly lies: in the legal containment of a private power that is structurally preponderant over the consumer <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 42; p. 162)</2>.

Objective good faith does not enter as decorative moralism, but as a technique for limiting the abusive exercise of private prerogatives, especially when projected onto a structurally vulnerable consumer <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 111; p. 221)</2>.

Marques formulates this shift by stating that, in consumer societies, "it is no longer believed that by ensuring the autonomy of the will and contractual freedom the necessary harmony and equity in contractual relations will automatically be achieved", stressing that standardized methods of contracting make "the imbalance between the contracting parties clear", which is why it fell to the State to intervene to restore balance and equality of forces <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 42)</2>.

Along the same lines, Marques defines abusiveness as "imbalance or mismatch of rights and obligations between the parties", associated with the authorization of conduct contrary to good faith and with the abuse of the preponderant contractual position <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 162)</2>.

This is exactly the point developed by Marques when she states that "the notion of objective good faith, as a new principle guiding the conduct of the contracting parties in captive contracts, means a new and important limitation on the exercise of subjective rights", so that the exercise of a right will be abusive when diverted from its economic and social function or exercised in disloyal circumstances <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 111)</2>.

The author adds that good faith has a limiting function, "reducing the freedom of action of the contractual partners" and controlling abusive conduct and clauses <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 221)</2>.

In relationships marked by vulnerability, dependence and continued trust, the rebalancing that can be required must reach fair and dignified treatment and protect legitimate expectations that go beyond a mere economic calculation <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 290; p. 1481)</2>.

It seeks, first and foremost, to materially restore the consumer's position, satisfy their interests and avoid greater harm, including in a non-pecuniary dimension <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1383; p. 856)</2>.

It is in this direction that Marques warns that "focusing only on the economic imbalance of the consumer contract would be a limited view of the notion of contractual equity", since what is sought is "the total rebalancing of the relationship, including its level of fair and dignified treatment", the only way to maintain and protect the legitimate expectations of the parties <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 290)</2>.

Along the same lines, the author observes that the principle of trust leads the CDC system to protect the adequacy, quality and reasonable safety of products and services, with the ultimate purpose "to improve the quality of life of Brazilians" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1481)</2>.

Marques, in addressing the legal guarantee of adequacy, stresses that it aims "to satisfy the interests" of the consumer, whether through the "perfect performance of the obligation", through the "rebalancing between the performances rendered", or through the avoidance of greater harm and compensation for harm already suffered, grounding this guarantee in the trust legitimately aroused and in the supplier's mandatory good faith in the market <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1383)</2>.

The author reinforces this reading by maintaining that, without an effective legal reaction to the frustration of trust and to the breach of ancillary duties, such commands would become "words in the wind", which is why the law of damages in the CDC fulfills not only a compensatory function but also a preventive and satisfactive one, reaching even non-pecuniary harm and negative interests <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 856)</2>.

Consumer law works with more open and functional concepts because they only gain meaning in light of the problem to be solved, and it is this key that prevents using the product-service dichotomy as an exclusionary filter of protection in continuous and governed digital supply <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 219-220; p. 149-150)</2>.

In long-term relationships, dependence may deepen to the point of frustrating relevant expectations if the relationship is interrupted or unilaterally reconfigured, which makes a reading centered only on superficial classificatory labels even less defensible <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 613; p. 109)</2>.

It is in this direction that Marques observes that consumer law moves away from the strict positivist ideal and adopts a problem-oriented style of thought, with concepts “more open, more functional, delimited without so much logical rigor”, precisely because “they only take on meaning in light of the problem to be solved” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 219-220)</2>.

In addressing the definition of consumer, the author states that “the rule of art. 2 must be interpreted in accordance with the special protection system of the Code and according to the purpose of the norm”, concluding that “only a teleological interpretation” makes it possible to define adequately the CDC's field of protection, including through openness to hypotheses in which vulnerability proves legally relevant, even if certain traditional classificatory fits do not appear in their purest form <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 149-150)</2>.
Even if the co-contracting party is a lawyer, a merchant or a farmer, factual vulnerability will almost always be present” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 613)</2>.

As the author records, these are services that “bind the consumer in such a way that, over the years of duration of the complex contractual relationship, the consumer becomes a ‘captive’ client of that supplier or chain of suppliers, becoming dependent on the very maintenance of that contractual relationship or seeing all their expectations frustrated.” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 109)</2> Applied to the present problem, this reading reinforces that the legal characterization of the relationship must take into account the real form of the supply and the vulnerability concretely produced by it, and not only formal labels that, used.

It is precisely this movement that describes the existence of "new contracts or contractual relationships" that, through adhesion contracts and general conditions, provide special services and create "complex long-term legal relationships", marked by the "position of 'captivity' or 'dependence' of the clients, consumers" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 77-78)</2>.

The maintenance of the relationship may lead the consumer to readily accept any new imposition by the supplier, guaranteeing the latter a constantly renewed "power of imposition" throughout the long-term obligation <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 109-110)</2>.

It is "a new view of the obligation, as a complex of acts, conduct, duties extending over time", with objective good faith being a source of duties "to inform, to cooperate, duty of care, of confidentiality, of advice, of loyalty etc." <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 110-111)</2>.

The long-term contract "carries within it expectations other than those of contracts of immediate performance", since it is based "more on trust, on repeated interaction, on the maintenance of the economic potential and the quality of the services", which is why "the capacity for adaptation, for cooperation between contracting parties, for continuation of the contractual relationship is basic" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1222)</2>.

Clauses imposed in relationships aimed precisely at future security and at the "maintenance of the contractually agreed promises and conditions" may represent "an excessive [...] discretionary power, placing the consumer at an excessive disadvantage contrary to good faith", allowing a factually "unilateral" variation of the content of the contract, of the performances and of the price <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1225)</2>.

In relational and captive contracts, revisions and readjustments cannot "authorize abuses of the dominant contractual position" or frustrate the legitimate expectations of the parties, and must operate according to cooperation, loyalty and good faith <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 101)</2>.

The contractual object cannot remain trapped in the image of the isolated material good, because protection already reaches quality, functionality, information, status and security ensured in the relationship <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 180; p. 183)</2>.

The contemporary consumer also accumulates immaterial goods linked to leisure, security, information, status and well-being, and consumer law already has instruments to offer reasonable answers to these cases without abandoning its own protective matrix <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 70-71; p. 104)</2>.

Marques synthesizes this shift by stating that, in the consumer contract, "what becomes important is the nexus of the performances and their balance (synalagma), not the performance itself, but its accessories, its quality, its functionality, the information that accompanies it, the status it ensures, the speed and security in its rendering." <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 180)</2>.

The CDC system, supported by the theory of the social function of the contract, focuses on the effect of the contract, so that the service rendered must be adequate for the purposes reasonably expected of it <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 183)</2>.

It is in this direction that Marques states that the adequate answer does not lie in "proclaiming the uselessness of the traditional scientific instruments of law", but in the "use of the legal instruments we have, especially the new Consumer Protection Code and the constitutional guidelines, so as to give reasonable and just answers to concrete cases" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 70-71)</2>.

The contemporary consumer tends to become an accumulator of services, activities and "immaterial goods" as well, linked to well-being, security, leisure, status, information and credit, which requires the law to keep pace with this change <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 104)</2>.

The consumer's vulnerability remains the pillar of the CDC's special protection, and it is precisely for this reason that semiotic vulnerability must be understood as a contemporary specification of this structural fact, and not as a parallel or extravagant category <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 324; p. 307)</2>.

The consumer's autonomy depends on positive duties to inform, to cooperate and to act with loyalty and care, because without this minimum level of conduct the decision to contract is not rational in any legally relevant sense <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 812; p. 1480)</2>.

One of the parties is vulnerable (art. 4. I), it is the weaker pole of the contractual relationship, since it cannot discuss the content of the contract", and, as a rule, it is left only to accept or reject the pre-set package <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 324)</2>.

The author adds that the definition of consumer constitutes "the pillar that sustains the special protection", because that protection exists only because of the vulnerability of the consumer party in market relations <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 307)</2>.

Marques makes this mechanism explicit by stressing that the idea of "rational autonomy" depends precisely on the application of ancillary duties to inform, to cooperate and to treat the consumer with loyalty and care, since only with this "new level of conduct in the market" can a "truly reflected, autonomous and 'rational" will of the consumer be achieved <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 812)</2>.

Along the same lines, the author states that the CDC seeks "transparency and harmony in consumer relations", imposing good faith as a requirement to prevent market practices from "taking advantage of the vulnerability of consumers", with the duty to inform being "a basic duty of suppliers" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1480)</2>.

Communicational asymmetry, therefore, is not resolved by proof that the text was "there", but by assessing whether its content was knowable in real terms for the average consumer, especially in contexts of strong unilateral predisposition: "the simple mention that GCTs will be used in the contract is not enough, it is necessary that the common man be able to read and understand what those clauses mean, what obligations and rights he is accepting" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 91-92)</2>.

The principle of transparency governs the pre-contractual moment and the very conclusion of the contract, being "more than a simple formal element", since it "affects the essence of the transaction", as information "forms part of the content of the contract or, if it fails, represents a failure in the quality of the product or service offered" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 819)</2>.

For this reason, the new function of contract law places the principle of interpretation in accordance with good faith back in a central position, so that art. 47 of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1>, together with the general clause of art. 51, IV, allows predisposed clauses to be interpreted "in a manner that respects the trust and the legitimate interests of the consumers who accepted these pre-drafted clauses" <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 94-95)</4>.

Breach of the duty of clear drafting is sanctioned by art. 46 of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1>, according to which contracts do not bind the consumer if they are drafted in a way that hinders understanding of their meaning and scope, a sanction that originates in the "presumption of bad faith of the supplier who drafted the contract" <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 902-903)</4>.

Marques offers decisive support by stating that good faith, concretized in the consumer relationship, "means mandatory transparency toward the contractual partner, a mandatory respect for the normal interests of the other contracting party, a positive action by the stronger contractual partner to allow the weaker contractual partner the conditions necessary for the formation of a free and rational will", adding that ensuring information, protection against pressure from sales methods and time for reflection are legal objectives of this pursuit of a rational consumer decision <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 812)</2>.

Along the same lines, the author maintains that the possibility of prior knowledge of the contractual text and of the obligations it contains is an "essential condition for the formation of a truly free, conscious, 'rational will", which is why art. 46 allows the consumer to ask a court for release from the bond when the supplier fails its duties of information <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 898-899)</2>.

Marques formulates this reasoning by stating that, in the face of the structural "pressures" that unbalance contracting in consumer society, the need arises for a "rebalancing legal response", exemplified by control of the content of the contract, by "a new informational formalism" and by the right of withdrawal without cause, all this "with the aim of rebalancing or making up for the 'factual failure' in the freedom or will of the weaker contracting party." <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 287)</2>.

The author also highlights the tendency of the courts to declare contractual clauses, and even entire consumer relationships, ineffective on the basis of arts. 46 and 54, § 4, of the CDC<1><2>4</2></1>, precisely because of problems of form and contractual drafting that reveal insufficient information and warning given to the consumer <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1304)</4>.

Marques makes this point explicit by stating that, given the legal guarantee of adequate and quality performance, “the norms of the CDC end up reaching the entire chain of suppliers involved, directly or indirectly, in satisfying the legitimate contractual expectations of consumers”, imposing protection of the trust aroused in the consumer group by the suppliers' conduct <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 991)</2>.

Marques states plainly that “the need to protect the freedom of the weaker contracting party leads to imposing new professional risks on suppliers, which cannot be transferred to consumers by any valid manifestation of will” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 274)</2>.

The author adds that the market's “contractual engineering” tends to be designed so as to transfer risks and duties to the partner in a non-dominant or more vulnerable position, but that “the risk of frustration of the contract should not be borne only by the consumer”, on pain of excessive advantage and destruction of contractual balance <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1185)</2>.

This is exactly the point made in interpreting art. 31 of the CDC<1><2>5</2></1>, which holds that the supplier must provide the consumer with “clear, precise and conspicuous information about the main characteristics of the product”, including data on its characteristics, its economic impact, health and safety <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 877)</4>.

As a reflection of the principle of transparency, the supplier must offer “clear and correct” information about the qualities of the product and the conditions of the contract, drafting the text clearly so as to “give the consumer the opportunity” to know the content of the obligations assumed, on pain of the contract not binding them, “even if duly formalized” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 820-821)</2>.

No average consumer could understand obligations assumed in contracts that pile up references to laws and provisional measures in an incomprehensible way, which is why such a bond may be undone for failure of transparency (in this case good faith) at the time of its formation, since the consumer could not understand what obligations they were assuming <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 903)</2>.

For general conditions to be incorporated, “the simple mention” that they will be used “is not enough”; the consumer must “be able to read and understand” what the clauses mean, and such texts often appear in a “somewhat furtive” way, in long or hard-to-read material <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 91-92)</2>.

Marques states that, in advertising, objective good faith requires it to be “a fair activity”, judged also from the standpoint of whoever receives the message, so that it promises only what it can deliver and, if it conveys information about characteristics of the product, the service or the contractual conditions, that this information is correct and truthful <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 832; p. 886)</2>.

The author adds that the main characteristic of misleading advertising, under the CDC, is that it is capable of leading the consumer into error, including through “omissions”, and that the rule must be interpreted broadly, since the error consists of a “false notion of reality” potentially formed in the consumer's mind by the advertising <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 909)</2>.

The meaning of the transparency mandate can be traced back to the search for the “true and free will of the consumer”, functioning as a “precondition” for them to freely express their will and realize their legitimate expectations, that is, those that led them, “duly informed about the product or service, aware of their future contractual rights and duties”, to choose a given supplier as contractual partner <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 818-819)</2>.

The interpreter of the consumer contract must observe not only the rule of art. 47 of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1>, but all the norms of the Code that establish rights and duties of consumer and supplier, so that “the content of the contract to be interpreted is not only that ‘set out’ in clauses pre-drafted unilaterally by the supplier, but also the entire prior context that constitutes the offer”, such as advertising, brochures, information and commercial practices <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1015)</4>.

This contextual interpretation seeks the meaning of the contract also in its negotiating context, considering prior acts and information as legally relevant and forming the whole to be considered <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1030)</2>.

The time lapse between the birth of the obligation and the satisfaction of the main performance “can no longer be seen as an ‘empty space’”, since the obligational relationship constitutes “a continuous whole”, within which the parties are bound by ancillary duties of conduct arising from objective good faith, among them “the duty to inform, to cooperate, duty of care, of confidentiality, of advice, of loyalty etc.” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 110)</2>.

Breaching the duty of cooperation and loyalty means failing to perform, even if partially, including when the supplier hinders the consumer's access to their rights <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 236)</2>.

The long-term contract “carries within it expectations other than those of contracts of immediate performance”, since it is based “more on trust, on repeated interaction, on the maintenance of the economic potential and the quality of the services”, which is why “the capacity for adaptation, for cooperation between contracting parties, for continuation of the contractual relationship” is essential <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 106)</2>.

The theory of the relational contract contributes to “a new understanding of the trust aroused by the suppliers' activity” and to the acceptance of constant readjustment of long-term relationships “so as not to frustrate the legitimate expectations of the parties” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 101)</2>.

For this reason, readjustments and mutations are legally admissible, yes, but only insofar as they are compatible with maintaining the expected utility and with not frustrating the legitimate expectations that sustained joining and remaining in the relationship <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 101)</2>.
If the fundamental legitimate expectations that underpinned the contract are excluded, the imbalance is no longer a detail: it becomes structural <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 292)</2>.

Changes that hollow out the utility, the quality or the material position of the consumer in the relationship may constitute, even under the appearance of continued acceptance, a form of factually unilateral variation of the contract incompatible with good faith <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1225; p. 1251; p. 1319-1320)</2>.

The new relevance of the time factor in long-term captive relationships is reflected “in the imposition of a new level of maintenance of the bond”, adding that, in this type of contract, the consumer's legitimate interest is directed toward the continuity of the relationship and, in principle, toward its renewal occurring “on the same terms and conditions as the initial policy” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1233)</2>.

Legitimate expectations form the “minimum (objective) basis of the relationship, of the consumer contract”, so that, with these expectations excluded, “the imbalance of the relationship is flagrant” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 292)</2>.

The theory of the relational contract contributes “to a new understanding of the trust aroused by the suppliers' activity and to the acceptance of a constant readjustment of long-term relationships so as not to frustrate the legitimate expectations of the parties, despite the limited will initially expressed.” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 101)</2>.

In relationships marked by practical dependence and strong preponderance of the supplier, the so-called supervening “consensus” frequently amounts to no more than forced adhesion, constituting a termination agreement contrary to good faith and fraud against the law because it allows the factually unilateral variation of the content, the performances, the quality or the price <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1225)</2>.

Clauses that authorize the supplier to unilaterally modify “the content of the contract or the quality of the contract” after its conclusion are abusive, as are practices that leave to its discretion the alteration of the performances or the price over time <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1251; p. 1319-1320)</2>.

If breaching the duty of cooperation and loyalty already means failing to perform, even if partially, then communication designed to neutralize useful understanding of the change also violates the regime of the relationship <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1242)</2>.

When the company modifies content, quality, parameters or relevant conditions of enjoyment, it must offer ample, intelligible and timely information, precisely because the consumer is placed in a relationship of practical dependence in which the cost of exit, adaptation or challenge is not neutral <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1319-1320)</2>.

The relational structure offered to the consumer must allow them, cooperatively, to understand relevant changes, access essential information and challenge decisions without artificial barriers, since excessive difficulties that prevent performance of the main obligation mean breach of duties of conduct under good faith: "breaching the duty of cooperation, of loyalty, means failing to perform, even if partially." <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1242)</2>.

Significant changes cannot be implemented through generic communications or communications structured to convert silence into fictitious acceptance, a practice considered abusive because it authorizes the unilateral modification of the content or quality of the performances after the conclusion of the contract <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1319-1320)</2>.

Even when companies intend to use such mechanisms, they must ensure ample information and a reasonable period for the consumer, or else they exploit the passivity and practical dependence inherent in contracts of continued performance <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1319-1320)</2>.

Good faith and balance operate precisely on this plane, making it possible to identify abuse when contractual or procedural engineering concentrates excessive unilaterality and significant imbalance to the detriment of the consumer <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 163; p. 291)</2>.

It suffices that the contractual or procedural structure operates as a mechanism of substantial imbalance, unjustifiably hindering the consumer's access to what would ordinarily be due to them <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1236)</2>.

Marques offers a decisive basis for this reading by stating that the interpreter's activity in identifying abusiveness must focus on a “dynamic and total view of contracts”, so that abusiveness is not observed in the isolated reading of the clause, but “in the reading of the whole contract, in the function of the clause in the contract as drafted, in the repercussion of the clause in that kind of contract” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 163)</2>.

The author reinforces that, under the influence of good faith, abuse may also be identified in the “excessive unilaterality or unreasonable imbalance of contractual engineering”, with the “significant imbalance of rights and duties, to the detriment of the consumer, in the contractual relationship seen as a whole” being an indication of abuse <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 291)</2>.

Marques is precise in stating that the attempt to prevent performance may be directed at the supplier's own performance, when the contract makes it enforceable only after “certain and multiple authorizations, papers, proofs, without plausible justification, merely to hinder and discourage the consumer from asserting their own (and main) claim.” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1236)</2>.

Claudia Lima Marques shows that the “barrier clause” is contrary to art. 51, IV, of the CDC<1><2>6</2></1>, precisely because it substantially unbalances the contractual relationship <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1236)</4>.

In continued relationships, this dynamic gains special relevance because the consumer finds themselves progressively more captive to the maintenance of the relationship and less free to resist new impositions by the supplier, who renews its power of influence precisely through the continuity of the relationship <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 109)</2>.

Pressure ceases to be a mere psychological fact and becomes part of the legally relevant relational framework itself, because the supplier exercises its power in an environment in which the continuity of the relationship becomes a good in itself for the consumer and the threat of rupture or impoverishment of this continuity comes to operate as a method of subjection <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 285-286)</2>.

Certain services and complex long-term relationships bind the consumer in such a way that they become dependent on the maintenance of the contractual relationship itself, on pain of seeing frustrated the expectations that led them to join and remain in the relationship: such relationships “bind the consumer in such a way that, over the years of duration of the complex contractual relationship, the consumer becomes a 'captive' client of that supplier or chain of suppliers, becoming dependent on the very maintenance of that contractual relationship or seeing all their expectations frustrated.” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 109)</2>.

This dependence reduces the consumer's real capacity to resist new impositions, guaranteeing the supplier a “power of imposition” constantly renewed throughout the long-term obligation <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 109)</2>.

In contracts for increasingly essential services, “pressure” takes on growing importance in the resolution of contractual conflicts, so that the exercise of certain rights by the professional in a position of power may constitute abuse of right or an act contrary to the good faith required in legal dealings, and this structural-social factor of pressure acquires new legal relevance in captive relationships <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 285)</2>.

The consumer's legitimate interest is directed toward the continuity of the contractual relationship, while the pressure may lie in the sales method itself, in marketing or in the object of the contract, and it is reflected in the final engineering of the relationship <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 285-286)</2>.

It is also recognized when the drafting party structurally improves its contractual position, transfers risks, unilaterally expands its power of control and breaks the minimum reciprocity that must sustain the consumer relationship <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1045)</2>.

The CDC responds to this not with contractual sentimentalism, but with objective nullity of excessive unilateral advantages, of the lack of minimum transparency and of the arbitrariness of one party over the other <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 161; p. 1319-1320; p. 1242)</2>.

Abusive clauses have in common the aim of improving the contractual situation of whoever holds the preponderant position and the effect of unbalancing the contract through lack of reciprocity <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1045)</2>.

The unilateral conception and drafting of the contract invites clauses that stand out for the unilaterality of the rights they secure, breaking the balance and weakening the consumer's contractual position <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 161)</2>.

Clauses that grant the supplier unilateral advantages, such as varying the price or canceling the relationship, without securing an equal right for the consumer are null, and the nullity arises from the very unilaterality of the advantage granted <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1319-1320)</2>.
Abusiveness rests on objective factors such as unilaterality, the lack of minimum transparency and the arbitrariness of one party over the other <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1242)</2>.

The will expressed in a contract is no longer an isolated decisive factor, and clauses that seek to turn continued enjoyment into a revocable favor, hollowing out its legal density, are not self-justifying merely because they were predisposed in an adhesion contract <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1004; p. 1080-1081)</2>.

License, exclusivity or technological secrecy do not remove the relationship from the consumer law regime when there is continued supply under exploitable vulnerability <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 471; p. 481; p. 612)</2>.

In consumer relations, the binding force of the text is not measured only by formal acceptance, but by its compatibility with good faith and contractual balance, since “the will of the parties freely expressed in the contract is no longer the decisive factor for the Law” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1004)</2>.

Art. 51, IV, of the CDC<1><2>6</2></1> functions as a general clause prohibiting provisions that establish iniquitous obligations or obligations incompatible with equity <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1080-1081)</4>.

The consumer microsystem establishes “a new legal regime for all kinds of contracts [...] involving consumers and suppliers of goods or services”, applying to all types of contracts, if they are consumer contracts <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 471; p. 481)</2>.

To characterize the consumer contract, the decisive factor is not the existence of a special law or the name given to the transaction, but the presence of a consumer in a materially protectable position <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 612)</2>.

The social function of property and of the contract thus acts as a vector of rebalancing, preventing the ownership of exclusive rights from being turned into a tool of oppression, of hollowing out enjoyment or of neutralizing the trust legitimately created in the relationship <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 235)</2>.

Marques associates this principle with the pursuit of contractual justice and balance, stating that the social function of the contract imposes limits on the freedom to contract in favor of the social interest, protecting trust and objective good faith <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 235)</2>.

Barbosa also shows that the software regime bears on maintenance, technical support, the development of improvements and the introduction of modifications to the original program, observing that there are circumstances in which access to the source code becomes necessary not only for discretionary changes, but also for correcting errors and updating the software for the purposes for which it was licensed <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 1959)</2>.

Barbosa underlines exactly this point by observing that one of the major debates in intellectual property applied to software stems from the fact that the program's primary source of value lies not in the text itself, but in its behavior, since different code can lead to identical functional results <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 1899)</2>.

While recognizing that copyright protection is not limited to the literal expression of the instructions, and may also reach the way the elements composing the software are organized, Barbosa warns that, “to the extent that the internal form is directly related to functionality, it will not be protected by Copyright”, since the latter “does not protect the structure in itself”; in other words, “the copyright protection of the program does not extend to the method of operation” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 1890)</2>.

It is precisely for this reason that legal scholarship identifies in design a dimension of “power of seduction”, capable of making the product more aesthetically attractive and thereby adding to its commercial value <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 21)</2>.

As Barbosa observes, it operates not in the realm of utilitarian needs nor in the field of technology, which belongs to patents, but in the space of commerce, that is, in the sphere of the public's choice and of marketing differentiation <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 68)</2>.

Hence the relevance of the notion of “commercial novelty”, mobilized by the author to show that industrial design is not intended to protect the functioning of the product, but its capacity to produce attraction and preference through singular aesthetic shaping <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 68)</2>.

Barbosa illustrates this didactically by observing that a plate ornamented with a given industrial design cannot be manufactured and sold by third parties without the holder's authorization, whereas the same plate, identical in size, material and functionality, but without that ornament, remains freely reproducible <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 50)</2>.

As the author notes, ornamental differentiation transcends the utility of the objects to which it is applied, allowing two cups identical in material and practical function to become completely distinct at the moment of purchase solely because of the sensory form that clothes them <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 39)</2>.

In a related formulation, Barbosa stresses that what sets industrial designs apart is that this differentiation forms part of the product itself, and does not merely signal it externally, as happens with other legal institutions <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 42)</2>.

According to Barbosa, the constitutional regulation of the cumulation of protections presupposes that each form of exclusive right fulfills a determined role, aimed at remunerating and organizing a specific type of creative investment, so that the ornamental function is distinguished, in the system, from both the expressive function and the technological function <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 45)</2>.

The difference lies in how each operates: in the trademark, distinctiveness signals; in the industrial design, differentiation forms part of the very visual shaping of the product <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 42; p. 68)</2>.

On the contrary, it is already captured by the system when the aesthetic appearance of the good comes to function as a competitive asset, endowed with power of seduction, commercial novelty and the capacity to guide the public's preference <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 21; p. 68)</2>.

Its function is more precise: to show that the legal system itself already recognizes, in an institutional key, that ornament is value, that aesthetic seduction is economically operative and that the form in which the good presents itself to the public may form part of the legally relevant core of the market experience <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 21; p. 39; p. 45; p. 68)</2>.
The principle remains that of freedom; exclusivity is a functionally delimited exception <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 84; p. 537; p. 547)</2>.

The very exercise of copyright may be abusive, and the patent, as an instrumental monopoly, coexists with mechanisms of containment and with the logic of exhaustion, which prevents endless control over every subsequent form of enjoyment of a good already placed on the market <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 110; p. 639; p. 671)</2>.

Not even the international regime enshrines a totalizing paradigm; it works, on the contrary, with a balance between incentive and diffusion, between protection and limits <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 75-76; p. 662)</2>.

The industrial result as such remains outside patent protection, which rules out treating the utility the consumer perceives as if it were wholly captured by the technological title <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010b, p. 1128)</2>.

Once on the market, certain subsequent effects escape the reach of exclusivity, and insisting on controlling them as if everything were still a natural extension of the title may constitute abuse of right <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010b, p. 1145; p. 1139)</2>.

The formal contractual relationship with the user has become a central mechanism for structuring access, and adhesion contracts often sharply limit the freedom to use the program <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 2011; p. 2018)</2>.

Exclusivity is not a safe-conduct for turning technical infrastructure into an unrestricted instrument for materially suppressing the contract's utility or neutralizing control over its effects <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 2025; p. 2030; p. 2026)</2>.

The know-how contract and the protection of secrecy explain specific ways of organizing power between the parties, but their legitimacy depends precisely on structuring through obligations and on concretely delimiting what is to be kept secret <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 361; p. 376)</2>.

Wherever there are effects on enjoyment, restoration or challenge, the protection of secrecy coexists with a minimum duty to make controllable whatever is to be invoked against the consumer and the system of protection <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 392-393)</2>.

Barbosa puts this directly when he states that each of these exclusive rights, although it constitutes property at the constitutional level, “exists within the limits and for the functions constitutionally assigned to it”, having not only the common social function but also a specific function in the design of intellectual property rights <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 84)</2>.

This structural limitation is reinforced when the author places exclusivity back within an economy of freedom: freedom is the principle, and the norm that removes certain creations from common use is the exception <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 537)</2>.
In intellectual property, “everything that is not protected is free to be copied, even slavishly” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 547)</2>.

Barbosa is explicit in recognizing that the very exercise of copyright may constitute abuse, precisely because it is subject to the constitutional limitations inherent in the social function and to restrictions arising from collision with other protected interests <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 110)</2>.

The patent, as an “instrumental monopoly”, does not survive as sovereign discretion and admits means of containment such as compulsory licensing and price control <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 639)</2>.

Moreover, under the doctrine of exhaustion, once the economic benefit has been obtained by placing the good on the market, the holder's rights over that copy cease, leaving only the exclusivity of reproduction <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 671)</2>.

Barbosa maintains that it is “even more functional, even more conditioned, even more socially responsible, and surely much less full than any other form of property” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 75)</2>.

This formulation blocks the reasoning by which the mere presence of an IP right would close the discussion of the limits on its exercise, since even absolute rights are technical categories that depend on normative configuration, not metaphysical expressions of sovereignty <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 75-76)</2>.

The departure from absolutism is explicit in the international regime, since the TRIPS Agreement does not enshrine an absolutist paradigm but rests on a balance between promoting innovation and diffusing technology <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 662)</2>.

Barbosa makes this point explicit by reconstructing the doctrine according to which the means of the invention correspond to the technical elements that solve a given problem, whereas “in relation to the result, it is not patentable” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010b, p. 1128)</2>.

The containment appears even more directly in the statement that “the industrial result will never be covered by the patent, always remaining free of the monopoly” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010b, p. 1128)</2>.

Once the product is placed on the market, “any subsequent use is outside the right of intellectual property”, and the relationship between holder and user moves to the ordinary plane of civil or commercial law <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010b, p. 1145)</2>.

Trying to enforce the exclusive right against the end user after exhaustion “would go beyond the reach of the patent” and would amount to “abuse of right” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010b, p. 1145)</2>.

This containment reinforces that the technical knowledge intrinsic to the patent remains freely usable for “any intellectual purpose, whether scientific or non-industrial” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010b, p. 1139)</2>.

Given how easy reproduction is in material terms, practice came to rely on a “formal contractual relationship between the user and the holder of the program”, rather than on abstract enforceability alone <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 2011)</2>.

The license does not appear as a peripheral detail, but as a central instrument for organizing access; adhesion contracts tacitly bind the user and limit their freedom of use, prohibiting, for example, reproduction or separation of components <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 2018)</2>.

Under Brazilian law, the use of intellectual property rights to dominate the market or limit access may constitute an infringement of the economic order, in light of the constitutional protection of freedom of competition <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 2025)</2>.

Exclusivity is not a safe-conduct for turning technical infrastructure into an unrestricted instrument of exclusion, since “abuse of exclusive rights” is also prohibited, and the legal efficiency of the exercise of power must still be examined <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 2030)</2>.

No state agent may enforce abusive or restrictive clauses in a license contract, and provisions flatly incompatible with the legal order are inadmissible <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 2026)</2>.

The know-how contract allows the holder to structure a relationship in which it remains master of the competitive capacity, a dominion that stems not from erga omnes sovereignty but from contractual organization: the supplier is “the master between the parties” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 361)</2>.

Protection of the secret depends on outwardly expressing the intention to keep it confidential within legally structured relationships, which must be “regulated by obligation” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 376)</2>.

In the regime of secrecy as in that of patents, legal protection applies only to certain and determinate elements, so the subject of the secret must be concretely delimited for the statutory grounds of protection to be verified <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 392)</2>.

Failure to specify the cause of action regarding the secrets allegedly exploited undermines any finding of unlawfulness; what would be common knowledge and what would be genuine novelty of a confidential nature must be delimited <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 393)</2>.

Intellectual property, as a constitutionally protected species of property, exists within the limits and for the functions assigned to it, including a specific function tied to development and the social interest, which prevents it from being invoked as an absolute barrier against scrutiny of practices that harm the integrity of the supply and the consumer's position <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 84)</2>.

Functionalization is internal to the IP regime itself. It is a form of property even more conditioned, even more socially responsible and less full than other forms of property, precisely because the exclusive right exists to balance private interests in exploitation against public interests in access, progress and the socially useful circulation of the immaterial <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 75)</2>.

The protection of the holder is not an end in itself; it is legitimized precisely because it remains compatible with a broader arrangement of social reciprocity <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 662)</2>.

Each of the exclusive rights protected by the system “exists within the limits and for the functions constitutionally assigned to it”, having not only the social function common to all property but also a specific function in the design of intellectual property rights, aimed at the technological and economic development of the Country <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 84)</2>.

By its very nature and mode of constitution, intellectual property is “even more functional, even more conditioned, even more socially responsible, and surely much less full than any other form of property” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 75)</2>.

Barbosa stresses that the TRIPS Agreement does not enshrine an absolutist paradigm but rests on a commitment to balance between promoting innovation and diffusing technology, “so as to contribute to social and economic welfare and to a balance of rights and obligations” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 662)</2>.

Eros Grau <1>(2008)</1> provides the conceptual safeguard against both the liberal neutralization of private normativity and its hasty transposition into the category of the State, allowing it to be described as presupposed law with collective effects and, for that reason, requiring control criteria commensurate with its density.

Eros Grau's formulation offers direct conceptual support for this framing when he maintains that “law” may mean a “system of principles (norms) coercively imposed on a given social group by any social organization endowed with the power to do so” <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 15-16)</2>.

Grau makes this shift explicit when he states that “the State is not the only social organization capable of positing law, that is, of producing posited law”, breaking “definitively with the conception according to which law is necessarily a creature of the State” <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 78)</2>.

In this sense, the warning that “the legal order of the market prevails”, understood not as something the market ontologically is but as “the order it establishes” <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 326)</2>, blocks readings that would treat private normativity as the mere spontaneous outcome of exchanges.

At the same time, once law is understood as “a level of the social whole […], in which social relations are expressed” <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 54)</2>, internal rules, architecture and enforcement can be treated not as an external representation of the conflict but as the very institutional materiality in which digital relations are formed, stabilized and given meaning.
Thus, as a level of reality itself, it is a constitutive element of the mode of social production” <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 19-20)</2>.

Following Grau <1>(2008)</1>, this institutional datum may be described as practical normativity, that is, a way of guiding conduct and imposing conformity that produces concrete effects without depending on state status.

The same idea appears in the statement that the State is not the only social organization capable of positing law, that is, of producing posited law, and that one must break with the conception according to which law is necessarily a creature of the State <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 78)</2>.
Grau makes clear that the expression “legal order of the market” means that the market posits its legal order, not the order it is but the order it establishes <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 324)</2>.

Moreover, this reading avoids an unproductive sociologization by recognizing that law is not a mere external representation of social reality but a functional level of the social whole and a constitutive element of the mode of social production <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 19-20)</2>.

In Eros Roberto Grau, the contractual relationship is described as the expression of an economic relationship that, whether or not legally regulated, already operates as a relationship of will, whose content is determined by the economic relationship itself <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 61)</2>.

Grau describes a two-way street, stating that presupposed law springs from society and conditions the making of posited law, but that positive law, when it applies, modifies presupposed law <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 64)</2>.

Discussing, with Duguit, how the rule of law is formed, Grau indicates that a social norm becomes a legal norm when the mass of consciences understands that the sanction can be “socially organized” <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 73)</2>.
The same intuition appears when Grau observes that the market posits its legal order by establishing an order it produces <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 326)</2>.

The constitutional text does not set economic freedom on one side and heterogeneous social limits on the other; it stitches these elements together within the same normative matrix, so that social function, social justice, consumer protection and the repression of abuse are not accidents of the system but its skeleton <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2010, p. 213; p. 252)</2>.

Free enterprise, in this framework, is neither a metaphysical right of capital nor a screen for corporate sovereignty, but a category functionally conditioned by constitutional purposes and by the protection of the person <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2010, p. 204; p. 208-209)</2>.

As such, its presence does not interrupt the constitutional logic of the market; on the contrary, it takes part in defining the legitimate way of organizing it, both as an instrument for achieving a dignified existence and as a specific constitutional objective to be promoted, including through public policy <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2010, p. 253)</2>.

The internal position of consumer protection becomes even clearer once one recognizes that it applies not only to pathological episodes or extreme abuses but structurally shapes the exercise of economic activity in the broad sense <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2010, p. 253-254)</2>.

Its normative meaning depends precisely on the articulated coexistence of free enterprise, free competition, the social function of property, consumer protection and the repression of abuse of economic power, principles that shape one another within the same constitutional matrix <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2010, p. 213)</2>.

Including both among the principles of the economic order does not signal mere rhetorical coexistence but a genuine subordination of the exercise of property to the dictates of social justice and to the objective of ensuring a dignified existence for all <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2010, p. 252)</2>.

For this reason, economic practices incompatible with valuing human labor, with social justice or with the general dignity that art. 170 aims at are not merely debatable business choices; they run counter to the constitutional order itself <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2010, p. 197)</2>.

The corresponding constitutional notion is not exhausted by economic freedom in the classic liberal sense, nor can it be read as a mere ideological affirmation of capitalism <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2010, p. 204)</2>.

This containment becomes even sharper when one observes that the Constitution enshrines the social value of free enterprise, not its individualist potential, and that art. 170 places it alongside human labor in a structure aimed at valuing the latter <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2010, p. 208)</2>.

For the same reason, free enterprise is taken neither as a fundamental right of the capitalist nor as a metaphysical attribute of capital, but as a category functionally tied to business activity within a constitutionally shaped context <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2010, p. 209)</2>.

Debord formulates this perspective by stating that the spectacle is not a collection of images, but a social relationship between people mediated by images <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 26])</2>.

This definition prevents the concept from being reduced to mass media, since the author refuses to treat it as a mere product of image-diffusion techniques and describes it as a worldview that has become effective and materially objectified <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 27])</2>.

Debord <1>(2013, [p. 120])</1> demystifies the supposed professional neutrality of the press and television by describing modern mass communication not as a space of dialogue, but as a vector of unilateral purity, in which discourse functions as administrative command.

Debord begins this diagnosis by stating that, in modern conditions of production, social life presents itself as an immense accumulation of spectacles and that everything that was directly lived has moved away into a representation <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 26])</2>.

The separation is structural, because the spectacle functions as the common language of the split itself, bringing individuals together without overcoming isolation, to the point of reuniting the separated and, even so, reuniting it as separated <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 33])</2>.

In this structure, exteriority is not limited to the content seen, since it reaches agency itself, insofar as one's own gestures are no longer one's own and come to be presented by another, which makes the spectacle ubiquitous and makes the subject feel at home nowhere <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 33])</2>.

Debord condenses this point by stating that the spectacle is the other face of money, as the abstract general equivalent of all commodities, and that in it the totality of use has already been exchanged for the totality of abstract representation <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 39- 40])</2>.

Debord condenses this mechanism by stating that the spectacle presents itself as an enormous, indisputable and inaccessible positivity and that its implicit rule is that what appears is good and what is good appears, requiring as a basic attitude a passive acceptance sustained by the monopoly of appearance <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 28])</2>.

In economic terms, this means that comparison need not operate on substantive criteria of enjoyment, since it can be organized as competition for administered distinctions, a “false choice” that unfolds as a “struggle of phantasmagorical qualities” meant to “impassion adherence” and to transfigure the occupation of “hierarchical places in consumption” into superiority <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 45])</2>.

When this dynamic is updated as a regime without reply, the very terrain of public verification contracts, since the mere fact of being, from then on, without counterpoint confers a new quality on the false, reduces the true to a hypothesis that can never be demonstrated and makes public opinion disappear as an autonomous force of validation <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 124])</2>.

The spectacle presents itself as indisputable and as if it were perpetual, but this claim is sustained only because it is founded on change and must change with its base, so that, for the author, nothing remains inert and this permanent movement constitutes its natural state <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 49])</2>.

In the later formulation of the integrated spectacle, this logic takes the form of a continuous present produced by the circular and ceaseless passage of information, which revolves around a few banalities reiterated as discoveries, creating speed without historicity and requiring constant repositioning within what is recognized as relevant <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 124])</2>.

In this regime, what gains the status of importance is the instantaneous, because the important tends to be so in the next instant and replaces another instantaneous importance, which produces a paradoxical eternity of successive non-importances, noisy and empty of fixation <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 125])</2>.

The economic density of this regime becomes explicit when Debord states that “the spectacle is capital to such a degree of accumulation that it becomes image” <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 34])</2>.

It is in this sense that, in all its particular forms, the spectacle constitutes the present model of socially dominant life, functioning as an omnipresent affirmation of the productive arrangement and having consumption as its corollary <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 27])</2>.

Debord condenses this active organization of wanting by stating that the spectacle wages a “permanent opium war” to make people accept the identification of goods with commodities and of satisfaction with survival, which must always increase precisely because it “never ceases to contain privation” <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 38])</2>.

Debord describes this mechanism as an “uninterrupted discourse” of the present order about itself, a monologue that, through the “fetishistic appearance of pure objectivity”, hides its character as a relationship between men and between classes and makes it seem that “a second nature” dominates the social milieu “with its fatal laws” <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 31])</2>.
Moreover, the spectacle operates by circular self-justification, converting its own means into an end <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 28])</2>.

The power of the spectacle, in Debord, consists in organizing the social totality as a field of evidence, in which the parameters of what can be recognized as real, relevant and legitimate are defined <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 28])</2>.
